topic.subject: social
topic.title: Gender, religion and caste in politics
topic.scope: gender division, women's representation, communalism, secular state, caste in politics

misconceptions.statement: The sexual division of labour is a natural biological necessity.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse social roles with biological traits.
misconceptions.fix: It is a social construct where domestic work is assigned to women and public work to men, not a biological requirement.

probe.question: Why do women do most of the housework?
probe.wrong_answer: Because they are naturally better at it.

misconceptions.statement: Women have 33% reservation in the Lok Sabha.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse local government reservation with national parliament reservation.
misconceptions.fix: Reservation for women exists in local bodies (Panchayats/Municipalities), but not yet in the Lok Sabha or State Assemblies.

probe.question: Is there reservation for women in the Indian Parliament?

misconceptions.root_belief: Rules apply uniformly across all levels

misconceptions.why: Students equate personal faith with political ideology.
misconceptions.fix: Communalism is the belief that followers of a particular religion must belong to one community and their interests are fundamentally opposed to others.

probe.question: What is communalism?
probe.wrong_answer: It means being very religious and following all rituals.

misconceptions.root_belief: A word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: A secular state must be anti-religious.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the Western model of separation with the Indian model of equal respect.
misconceptions.fix: The Indian secular state does not separate religion and state entirely but ensures equal distance and respect for all religions.

probe.question: Does a secular state ban religious symbols?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it must be neutral by removing all religion.

misconceptions.statement: Caste in politics always leads to negative outcomes.
misconceptions.why: Students over-focus on caste-based violence and ignore political representation.
misconceptions.fix: Caste in politics can also give marginalized groups a voice and power, leading to more inclusive decision-making.

probe.question: Is caste in politics always bad?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it only causes division and conflict.

misconceptions.root_belief: One event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Women's representation in politics is high in India because women vote in large numbers.
misconceptions.why: Students equate high voter turnout with holding office, so they conflate participation as voters with representation as elected members.
misconceptions.fix: Women's turnout is now close to men's, but women are still few among elected members: about 14% of Lok Sabha members and under 5% in many state assemblies.

probe.question: Women vote in large numbers in India. Does this mean women are well represented in the Lok Sabha?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because many women vote, they are well represented in Parliament.

misconceptions.root_belief: Voting participation equals representation in elected bodies
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Democratic Politics II, Ch. 4 and classroom assessment

misconceptions.statement: Gender division means only that boys and girls are biologically different.
misconceptions.why: Students use 'gender' and 'sex' interchangeably and miss that gender division is a social hierarchy of roles and status.
misconceptions.fix: Gender division is a social arrangement based on stereotyped roles, not biology. It shows up in unequal literacy, wages and sex ratio, and in the belief that public life is for men.

probe.question: What does gender division mean?
probe.wrong_answer: It means the natural physical differences between men and women.

misconceptions.root_belief: Gender is the same as biological sex
misconceptions.source_hint: Research on students' gender-sex concept confusion; NCERT Ch. 4

misconceptions.statement: Panchayats and municipalities have no reservation for women; reservation exists only in Parliament.
misconceptions.why: Students know reservation as a debated Parliament issue and miss that local bodies already have it.
misconceptions.fix: Since 1992-93 amendments, one-third of seats in rural panchayats and urban municipalities are reserved for women. Reservation for Parliament and state assemblies was a pending demand then.

probe.question: Where in India are one-third of seats reserved for women in elected bodies?
probe.wrong_answer: Only in the Lok Sabha; local bodies have none.

misconceptions.root_belief: Reservation applies only at the national level

misconceptions.statement: Communalism is a problem only of the majority religious community.
misconceptions.why: Students link communalism with riots by the majority and miss that any community can follow communal politics.
misconceptions.fix: Communalism is the idea that religion is the basis of social community and political interests. Any religious group, majority or minority, can practise it.

probe.question: Can a minority community's leaders also practise communal politics?
probe.wrong_answer: No, communalism is only done by the majority community.

misconceptions.root_belief: Communalism belongs to one kind of group
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Ch. 4 on communalism in various forms

misconceptions.statement: A secular state has an official religion chosen by the majority.
misconceptions.why: Students mix democracy as majority rule with secularism and assume the majority religion becomes the state religion.
misconceptions.fix: India has no official religion. The Constitution gives no special status to any religion and protects freedom to profess, practise and propagate any faith.

probe.question: Which religion is the official religion of India since most people follow it?
probe.wrong_answer: Hinduism, because the majority follows it, is the state religion.

misconceptions.root_belief: Majority rule means majority religion governs the state

misconceptions.statement: The caste system has disappeared from India because it is now illegal.
misconceptions.why: Students think that laws and urbanisation have ended caste in practice.
misconceptions.fix: Caste discrimination is banned and economic change has weakened some old practices. But caste identity still shapes marriage, jobs and politics, and inequalities remain.

probe.question: Does caste still matter in India after laws banned caste discrimination?
probe.wrong_answer: No, caste has completely vanished because the law made it illegal.

misconceptions.root_belief: A law banning a practice ends it
misconceptions.source_hint: NCERT Ch. 4 on caste inequalities today

misconceptions.statement: Elections in India are decided only by caste and a candidate wins if their caste has most voters.
misconceptions.why: Students see caste mentioned in electoral politics and turn it into the only cause of results.
misconceptions.fix: Parties consider caste composition, but voters also weigh party, performance, leaders and issues. Voters of one caste are not all united, and sitting governments often lose.

probe.question: Why does a party win in a constituency where one caste has the most voters?
probe.wrong_answer: Only because that caste has the most voters, so its candidate always wins.

misconceptions.root_belief: One social factor alone decides election outcomes
